flawed_step: The claim that a maximum flow always needs at least F+1 arcs with positive flow. That fails when s and t are joined by a direct arc, because each unit of flow can then use a single arc.
counterexample: Vertices {s, t, a, b}. There is one arc, s->t, with capacity 1; a and b are isolated, which the definitions allow. The graph has no loops and s != t. The cut ({s,a,b},{t}) has capacity 1, so F = 1 > 0. The only arc is s->t, so every flow puts flow only on it. The maximum flow f(s->t) = 1 is therefore the only maximum flow, and it puts positive flow on 1 arc. But F+1 = 2, so the conclusion fails.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. Take 4 vertices where the only arc is s->t, with capacity 1. Then F = 1, and the only maximum flow puts positive flow on 1 arc, which is fewer than F+1 = 2.
